title: Sephiria Weapons & Upgrades (1.0) — Six Branches, Tier Notes, Routes
description: Sephiria weapons guide: the six branches compared, how weapon upgrade offers work, the 50+ upgrade trees, evolution routes and branch unlock steps.
meta: Covers sephiria weapons / weapon upgrades / tier list / unlock dagger intent at branch level. Six branches only; no scaling figures and no current tier order.
body:
Sephiria has six weapon branches, and each one carries a deep upgrade tree — the store listing advertises more than 50 unique upgrades per weapon. There is no seventh starter weapon: the scythe people search for is a Dagger conversion, explained on the scythe page.

The six branches at a glance

WeaponIdentityBest fitMain tradeoff
Sword and ShieldDefensive close meleeFirst runs and pattern learningShort reach
GreatswordHeavy, wide meleeCreating space and clearing groupsLong commitment per swing
DaggerFast reaction meleePrecise counters and bossesExtremely short reach
CrossbowRanged positioningKiting and safe damageReload discipline
KatanaAggressive meleeHigh ceilings once parry timing is learnedSteeper mastery curve
Staff / QuarterstaffVersatile casterFlexible damage at most rangesWants upgrade support to scale

How to read the branch table

Three columns, three jobs. “Identity” is what the branch does when you press attack. “Best fit” is the situation the branch is listed for. “Main tradeoff” is the thing you notice on floor one, not in a highlight video. Nothing in the table is ranked, and the figure note says so deliberately: the branch you commit to should match the run in front of you.

The tradeoff column is the one that decides runs. Short reach, long commitment per swing, reload discipline, a mastery curve and upgrade dependence are five different kinds of cost, spread across six branches. Pick the one you can work around for a whole climb rather than the one with the best ceiling on paper.

Pick order by what you want from the run

If this is your situationStart withWhy, from the table
First runs, still learning patternsSword and ShieldListed for first runs and pattern learning; the cost is short reach
You want space and group clearsGreatswordHeavy, wide melee for creating space; the cost is a long commitment per swing
You want precise counters on bossesDaggerFast reaction melee; the cost is extremely short reach
You would rather not stand in meleeCrossbowRanged positioning and kiting; the cost is reload discipline
You want the highest ceiling and will pay for itKatanaAggressive melee with a high ceiling once parry timing is learned; a steeper mastery curve
You want one answer at most rangesStaff / QuarterstaffVersatile caster for flexible damage; wants upgrade support to scale
You want the scythe from the videosDagger, then DrifaThe scythe is a conversion, not a branch — see the scythe page

Each row restates a cell from the branch table above. The order is by situation, not preference: two rows can be right for the same player on different nights.

How weapon upgrades actually work

  • Upgrades are offered, not bought. Each branch has a large pool — the advertised figure is more than 50 unique upgrades per weapon — and you pick from what the run shows you.
  • Offer rates differ by branch. Community 1.0 data reports Greatsword upgrades appearing more often than Dagger upgrades, which is why best also means actually completes.
  • Routes chain. An enhancement can convert one weapon skill into another: on Dagger, the frost line runs Dormant Frost into Drifa, and Drifa converts Blizzard Hammer into Blizzard Scythe.
  • Endpoints have names. Community routes end at named evolutions — Frozen Smelt from the Dagger frost line, Minigun from the crossbow lightning line, Creaking Spine from the greatsword line, Biryuu on Katana, and the elemental fusion staff on the caster line.
  • Presets remember the shape. Once a run works, a preset lets you rebuild it without re-deriving every pick.

Upgrade routes people finish

RouteBranchSteps as the community writes them
Blizzard ScytheDaggerDagger → Dormant Frost → Drifa, which converts Blizzard Hammer into Blizzard Scythe
Frozen SmeltDaggerDagger → Sleeping Frost → Frozen Smelt
MinigunCrossbowHeavy Crossbow → Unstable Lightning Mark → Minigun
Creaking SpineGreatswordSteel Greatsword → Bone Mechanism Sword → Creaking Spine
BiryuuKatanaKatana → Biryuu
Formless DanceStaffStaff → Throwing Spear → Formless Dance
Elemental Fusion StaffStaffStaff → Flame Staff → Elemental Fusion Staff
Route names and intermediate steps come from community reporting at 1.0.x. If a step is never offered in your client, the pool has changed — the branch is still the thing to commit to.

Unlocking a branch (Staff example)

  1. Progress to the chapter that opens weapon training.
  2. Buy the weapon training node on the Destiny Inscription tree with Sapphires.
  3. Talk to the village training-ground NPC, finish the short training ground, and the weapon appears on the village rack.
Exact sapphire costs and node names shift between patches — confirm in your client Journal or Destiny UI before committing a save's Sapphires.

Are the tier lists trustworthy?

Tier lists for Sephiria disagree because they are editorial and version-bound. One 1.0 list puts Greatsword and Staff at the top and Sword and Shield near the bottom; a later 1.0.30 meta list reorders the same branches and puts Katana and Greatsword first. Both are community rankings, not official TEAM HORAY tiers.

Use them to pick a branch to learn, then judge by whether your offers complete a route — see the builds page for which routes people finish.

Offers decide whether a branch finishes

A branch is a commitment, but the run decides whether the commitment pays out. Upgrades are offered rather than bought, and community 1.0 data reports Greatsword upgrades appearing more often than Dagger upgrades. That one sentence is why “best” and “finishes” are different words on this page: a route that needs one specific second enhancement can stall if the pool never shows it.

Two consequences. Treat the route tables as destinations rather than shopping lists, because a step that never appears means the pool has changed and not that you played the branch wrong. And if you are still learning, favour a branch whose early offers are useful on their own rather than only as part of an endpoint. The named endpoints — Frozen Smelt, Minigun, Creaking Spine, Biryuu, the elemental fusion staff — are worth recognising because they tell you the run has arrived, not because they are the only way to play the branch.

Presets matter here more than they look. Once a run works, a preset rebuilds the shape without re-deriving every pick, which is how you test a second branch without losing the first.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a route table as a purchase order. Upgrades are offered, not bought, so a missing step means the pool changed.
  • Judging a branch by its endpoint name. The endpoint is the last step, not the reason the branch works.
  • Spreading picks across branches. The tree is deep — more than 50 upgrades per weapon in the store listing’s figure — and offers you never take are wasted floors.
  • Committing both enhancement slots to a conversion without a plan for the rest. The scythe route spends both slots on the frost line, which commits the run to it (scythe page).
  • Buying the training node and stopping there. The branch appears only after the training ground is finished and the weapon shows on the village rack.
  • Reading two tier lists and concluding the branches are broken. The lists disagree because they are editorial and version-bound; one reorders the same branches in a later patch.
  • Assuming a seventh weapon exists. Every official branch summary stops at six, so a scythe on screen is a Dagger run that reached Drifa.

What this page cannot confirm

  • Exact scaling per upgrade. No damage percentages or per-level values are published here; the route names and branch identities are the reliable part.
  • Offer probabilities. The only claim made here is the reported ordering between Greatsword and Dagger upgrades; nothing on the page quantifies the gap.
  • A current tier order. The lists cited are community rankings at a stated version, not an official ranking, and they disagree with each other.
  • Whether every listed step still exists. Steps come from 1.0.x community reporting; the branch is the durable commitment, the individual step is not.
  • Sapphire costs and node names. They shift between patches, so confirm in the Journal or the Destiny UI before spending.
  • Whether Hard Mode changes the offer pool. Nothing on this page or in its sources says so either way, so it stays open rather than guessed.

Where the rest of it lives

  • Turning a branch into a run — builds lists the setup names and the Artifact pairings players report.
  • The grid a branch amplifies — Artifacts and Tablets, including the Bond artifacts that need two tags at once.
  • Unlocking a branch in the first place — Destiny Inscription, for the training node and the Sapphire order.
  • The summoner route specifically — the Companion build, which also starts by picking a weapon and family before floor one.
  • Where branches get tested — bosses for the fight notes, and Hard Mode for what comes after a clear.
  • First-run basics — the beginner guide, including why Side Bag items are inactive.

Questions this page answers directly

Are there six weapons or seven?

Six. The store listing and every official branch summary stop at Sword and Shield, Greatsword, Dagger, Crossbow, Katana and Staff / Quarterstaff. The scythe is a Dagger conversion, explained on the scythe page.

Can I buy a specific upgrade?

No. Upgrades are offered and you pick from what the run shows you, which is why a route can stall even when you know the steps.

Why do people say Greatsword is easier to build?

Because of offer rates rather than damage. Community 1.0 data reports Greatsword upgrades appearing more often than Dagger upgrades, so Greatsword routes complete more reliably.

Which branch is best?

This page does not answer that, on purpose. Two 1.0 tier lists disagree and both are community rankings. Use them to pick a branch to learn, then judge by whether your offers complete a route.

How do I unlock the Staff?

Progress to the chapter that opens weapon training, buy the weapon training node on the Destiny Inscription tree with Sapphires, then finish the short training ground with the village NPC. The weapon then appears on the village rack.

Is Blizzard Scythe a separate weapon?

No. Dagger, then Dormant Frost, then Drifa converts Blizzard Hammer into Blizzard Scythe. That is a weapon skill on the Dagger branch, not a seventh starter.
